articleTitle: Subjective effects of transmitting speech over packet networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Packet switching is suitable for the transmission of most types of data, but it is not a natural medium for speech and at present there are no agreed standards on the way in which this should be done. To help determine some of the acceptable limits for such standards a series of experiments have been carried out. These examine some of the subjective effects of using packet networks as carriers of speech. Delays when sending/receiving packets over these networks are not usually critical for data, but they are not acceptable for speech. If speech packets are delayed for too long they must be assumed to be missing. Different methods have been proposed to cope with this loss of information. Listening tests have been run to determine the subjective effects of some of these methods, and to find what percentages of missing packets are found to be both detectable and objectionable to the listener.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated networks: the case for packets
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: The paper reviews the demands which a variety of services make on a single integrated service network. It shows why packet networks offer a suitable solution and gives examples. Packet networks offer a flexible alternative to circuit switching. In order to consider their suitability for integrated service networks it is necessary to consider the service requirements. A comparison of the transmission rate, nature, toleration of errors and toleration of delay for a number of services is given in a table, indicating some of the typically orthogonal requirements of information which has conventionally used circuit switched techniques and of data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Recognising that the future network will need to provide customers with a very broad and flexible range of services, the CCITT SG XVIII have recommended that ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) should be the basis of its implementation. ATM is an affordable way while opening up the possibilities for new, but as yet ill defined, broadband services. To take advantage of these new services requires the provision of broadband customer access. Thus the introduction of ATM is critically dependant on the introduction of optical fibre access systems. Some of the options for supporting broadband ATM connections and meeting the requirements of different services and customers are explored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: At the Hewlett Packard Research Laboratories in Bristol, the construction of a Gbit/s network is under way and will serve as a test-bed for experimentation with high speed and multi-service networks. The architecture of the system, along with the networking protocols used are described. An optical medium at the physical layer is used to support the high bit rates. A laser transmitter module operating at a wavelength of 1300 nm and a PIN/FET transimpedance optical receiver are used. The transmission medium is standard single mode optical fibre. The stations on the network are active-the optical signal is converted to an electrical signal, processed and converted back to an optical signal before transmission to the next station. The clock for transmission is regenerated at each station so that accumulation of jitter does not occur.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Voice data integration for a multiservice workstation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Integrated communications for multiservice workstations will have to support both asynchronous data traffic and delay sensitive traffic such as real time video and voice. In an initial step towards this, a system providing a telephone service integrated into PCs and communicating over an IEEE 802.3 LAN has been demonstrated. The further development of this digital voice station into a full communicating multimedia workstation is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integration of packet and circuit switching in the 1990's
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Explores new directions in the evolution of integrated packet and circuit switching. Widespread deployment of Broadband Integrated Services Digital Networks (B-ISDNs) employing Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) techniques is still some way off and consideration is limited to the pre-B-ISDN era. The trends observable in the current market for data and integrated voice/data networks are reviewed. The state of the standards in this area is then examined in relation to the trends. The author then takes a look at the more practical issues of current developments and the architectures of integrated circuit/packet switches. One particular development called the 'ISDN Additional Packet Mode Bearer Services' is examined in some depth.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated switching system: a distributed star network for integrated voice and data traffic
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Contains a brief introduction to the need for voice and data service integration, and the role played by the PBX in providing such an integrated facility in the local office environment. A description of a proposed integrated network, of which a prototype version has already been designed and built then follows, accompanied by a short discussion on the salient features which enable it to overcome some of the shortcomings associated with more traditional networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evolution strategies from the PSTN to the IBCN
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Integrated Multiservice Communication Networks
abstract: Demonstrates how the current network can evolve into a future network by adding functionality to the existing network. Many types of networks and network nodes may be generated by addition of elements to the existing network nodes. In examining how the PSTN (Public Switched Telephony Network) can evolve into part of the IBCN (Integrated Broadband Communications Network), it is first necessary to understand both the PSTN, and the proposed IBCN. Permitting the present network to evolve will place many constraints, and these may actually restrict the options for the new network. The requirement for evolution must be considered seriously, for if the new network can not be installed in an evolutionary manner, it can only be used for totally new services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
